byTheNumbers.standfirst: 960 million people, of whom half had electricity at home and fewer than one in a thousand used the internet.

items.title: Who could read
items.summary: At the 1991 census 43 to 52 percent of people could read and write, 53 to 64 percent of men and 32 to 39 percent of women.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: The first mobile calls and the first public internet connections came in August; most households were still waiting for a landline.

items.title: Telephones
items.summary: India had 5.07 million telephones in 1991, up from 0.98 million in 1971 and 2.15 million in 1981.

items.title: The first mobile service
items.summary: The first mobile telephone service started on a non-commercial basis in Delhi on 15 August 1995.

items.title: Public internet
items.summary: VSNL launched India's first public internet service, the Gateway Internet Access Service at 9.6 kbit/s, on 15 August 1995; an individual account cost ₹5,200 for 250 hours and an institutional dial-up account ₹16,200.

items.title: A policy for every village
items.summary: The National Telecom Policy of 1994 aimed to bring telephone facilities to all villages, set a target of one public call office for every 500 people in urban areas, and reserved 5 percent of new lines for PCO booths.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine

items.title: Pulse Polio
items.summary: In 1995, following the Global Polio Eradication Initiative, India launched the Pulse Polio programme of oral vaccine for children under five on national immunisation days.

items.title: The end of polio
items.summary: The last cases of wild polio in India were reported in West Bengal and Gujarat on 13 January 2011, and the WHO declared India polio-free on 27 March 2014.

items.title: A film that never left
items.summary: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge opened on 20 October 1995 and has been shown daily since at the Maratha Mandir cinema in Mumbai, reaching its 1,000th week in December 2014.

spotlight.title: Cable TV and the PCO booth
spotlight.standfirst: Cable and satellite television spread through towns before the law caught up, and a yellow booth with a telephone and a meter became the neighbourhood's long-distance line.

items.title: The Cable Act of 1995
items.summary: The Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, was passed to address the sudden growth of cable and satellite networks in the early 1990s; it required registration and a programme code and advertisement code, and operators to carry at least two Doordarshan channels and one regional-language channel.

sources.label: iPleaders: An analysis of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995
Jus Scriptum Law: Cable Television Network (Regulation) Act, 1995

items.title: Sixty thousand operators
items.summary: One estimate puts the number of cable operators at about 60,000 in 1995, of which later only 16,000 to 19,000 registered under the Act.

sources.label: iPleaders: An analysis of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995

items.title: From CNN to Zee
items.summary: The spread of cable is tied to CNN's Gulf War coverage in 1990, which created demand for satellite dishes, and to the launch of Star TV and Zee TV.

sources.label: IUP: The Indian cable TV industry
St. Xavier's/ SH College: History of Television in India (NAAC document)

items.title: The yellow booth
items.summary: Sam Pitroda's push under Rajiv Gandhi spread bright-yellow STD/PCO booths across India, giving a business to people who would otherwise have been unemployed.
